'某 department' opposed releasing data, revised 'Hong Kong Heat Index'

Lam Chiu-ying reiterated that wet bulb and black globe temperature indicators should be used. He recalled that the relevant formula was almost finalised back then, and the Hong Kong Observatory had prepared to release this data to the public, but was opposed by 'a certain department'. There were concerns that publicly releasing wet bulb and black globe temperatures might draw attention from the labour sector, so the Observatory was asked to develop another indicator that does not apply to outdoor situations — this became the 'Hong Kong Heat Index' currently cited by the government.

Says the two are absolutely not similar

Lam Chiu-ying pointed out that the two are absolutely not similar. The Hong Kong Heat Index sidesteps outdoor work situations and does not address exposure to intense sunlight. He noted that all data use three sets of figures — air temperature, black globe temperature, and wet bulb temperature — and the difference lies only in the weighting.

He gave the example of Japan, which adopts wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT). When it reaches 28 degrees or above and work exceeds one hour, any heatstroke incident must be 'filed as a case'. He said that nowadays 'warnings are issued too often', which instead makes the public 'feel confused'. He noted that some people believe that once the Observatory issues an extreme heat weather reminder, the red heat stress at work warning should be activated immediately, which could reduce public confusion. He said: 'All records have been broken, yet people are still blaming the Observatory for not issuing the red warning — this is out of touch, detached from reality.'

Labour and Welfare Bureau: mechanism to be reviewed

Under Secretary for Labour and Welfare Ho Kai-ming responded that the Labour Department will review the existing mechanism together with the Observatory and other departments to carry out the relevant work.
